KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Fantastic early fall weather continues midweek as we get into
weak return flow behind departing high pressure. Any fog
development tonight should be rather limited as a bit more of a
gradient will likely allow most locations to hang onto a light 
breeze, though some valleys may still decouple and see patchy
fog. Wednesday will feature an increase in clouds but should 
remain dry until the evening hours. Lows will generally dip into
the 50s tonight, with the light south-southwest breeze keeping
us a little milder than last night. The modest return flow will
support slightly warmer highs in the mid-upper 70s on Wednesday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A closed low (partially comprised of the remnants of East
Pacific Hurricane Polo) will eject out of the Southwest and into
the Plains Wednesday into Thursday, before shearing out/ 
weakening as it lifts towards the Ohio Valley on Friday. At the
same time, ridging over the eastern U.S. will flatten as a
shortwave moves through the northern Great Lakes and into New
England, pushing a cold front southeast across the local area
Thursday night into Friday. 

A loosely defined warm front is expect to lift across the area 
late Wednesday into Wednesday night. Increasing mid-level 
moisture and some isentropic lift along/ahead of the warm front
may support some rain showers late Wednesday through early 
Thursday, particularly across northern portions of the area. 
More models are indicating this potential than prior cycles, so 
have added some 20-40% type rain chances to the forecast. Rain 
amounts late Wednesday into early Thursday will generally be 
near or under 0.10", with locally up to 0.10-0.25" possible. 

Much of the day Thursday will be dry in the open warm sector, 
with rain lingering early towards Northwest PA closer to the 
warm front and approaching from the northwest late in the day 
ahead of the cold front. The greatest window for rain will be 
from northwest to southeast Thursday night into Friday. There is
some disagreement over how progressive the front will be, which
will influence how rainy we are through the day Friday and 
overall QPF amounts. The current forecast leans a soggier
direction for Friday, especially through the early afternoon,
with some potential for northern portions of our area to dry out
through the afternoon. Much of the area is expected to see
0.40-0.80" of rain Thursday night through Friday, with the
greatest amounts expected across Northwest Ohio. Somewhat
unintuitively, a slower front could lead to less overall QPF 
per ensemble members, as the overall system will be weakening 
with time. Regardless, ensembles suggest that a drier system 
producing as little as 0.20-0.50" overall is possible, with a 
more robust solution potentially dropping 1.00-1.50" in the 
Toledo area. Overall, this rain will be beneficial and should 
not pose a risk for impactful flooding falling on dry grounds. 

Highs will push towards 80 on Thursday, our last day with such
values for a while. Highs on Friday are forecast to range from
the mid 60s to near 70, though that may be slightly misleading
as highs will be early in the day ahead of the front, with
temperatures holding steady or falling behind the front. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
High pressure builds into the lower Great Lakes Friday night
into Saturday behind the departing front, bringing a period of
drier and somewhat cooler weather. Another potent shortwave is 
expected to dive through the Great Lakes and into New England 
Sunday and Monday, carving out a deeper trough over the 
Northeast. This will likely bring a re-enforcing/stronger cold 
front late Sunday or Monday that may be accompanied by a chance 
of showers, followed by an even cooler airmass the first half 
of next week. The overall airmass and high pressure strength 
may support a frost potential Monday night/early Tuesday, 
assuming favorable high placement for radiational cooling.
